full_judgment:
3. Mr. Formanullah Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the second party petitioners has taken me through the impugned judgments and orders of the courts below and other relevant materials. The learned Advocate has, as a preliminary point challenged the competency of the learned Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be an Additional Sessions Judge to hear the revisional application under section 439A Cr.P.C. The learned Advocate has, placed reliance on the decision of Md. Mostafa Mondal Vs. The State reported in 35 DLR 362 decided by a Single Judge of Rangpur Jurisdiction. Before considering the decision of the learned. Single Judge, I would consider the relevant provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code, The proviso to sub-section (3) of section 9 of the Cr.P.C. provides that where in a district, the District Magistrate, Additional District Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class is specially empowered under section 29C to try any offence, all Assistant Sessions Judges of the Sessions Divisions within which the District is situate shall be deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judges of that Division. By Notification No. ED/FA-52/82-466 dated 8.9.82 the Government invested all Additional District Magistrates with powers to try as Magistrate all offences not punishable with death or, with transportation or with imprisonment for a term exceeding 10 years. By another Notification No. ED/VA-28/83-120 dated 6-3-83 the Government invested all Additional District Magistrate with powers to try as Magistrate all offences not punishable with death. It, therefore, appears that all Additional District Magistrates within the territories of Bangladesh have been specially empowered under section 29C to try all offences not punishable with death and there is no dispute that all Assistant Sessions Judges of this country are now deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judges of their respective Sessions Divisions under the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 9 of the Code, Mr. Formanullah Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, however, submits that sub-section (4) of section 31 of the Cr.P.C. provides that an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be Additional Sessions Judge under the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 9 may pass any sentence authorised by law except the sentence of death and such Assistant Sessions Judge is deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judge only for the purpose of passing the enhancement sentence for the passing of which he is authorised under sub-section (4) of section 31. The learned Advocate submits that, except for the limited purpose of passing the enhancement sentence, such Assistant Sessions Judge cannot be deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judge. The learned Advocate submits that such Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge cannot hear revisional applications under section 439A Cr.P.C. Section 439A Cr. P.C. empowers an Additional Sessions Judge to hear revisional applications under section 439A in respect of cases which may be transferred to him by the Sessions Judge. The learned Advocate submits that sub-section (3) of section 439A does not categorically spell out that an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be an Additional Sessions Judge may also exercise the revisional powers. In Biswas's Encyclopedic Law Dictionary, the word "deemed" has been given the following legal meaning:- "Deem." The word "deemed" is used a great deal in modern legislation. Sometimes, it is used to impose for the purposes of a statute an artificial construction of a word or phrase that would otherwise prevail ................ 

 4. In view of the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 9 Cr.P.C. as soon as in any district, the District Magistrate, Additional District Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class is specially empowered under section 29C to try any offence, all Assistant Sessions Judges of the Sessions Division within which the district is situate are deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judges of that division. The Assistant Sessions Judges are not in fact appointed as Additional Sessions Judge, but by a legal fiction, they are deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge, with the result that the Assistant Sessions Judges deemed to be appointed as Assistant Sessions Judges may-exercise all the powers and discharge all the functions of the Additional Sessions Judges conferred upon the Additional Sessions Judges under the law, subject to any limitation as may be prescribed by the law itself. Sub-section (4) of section 31 Cr.P.C. prescribes such a limitation on the powers of an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judge, and the limitation is that an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge cannot pass a sentence of death. The limitation is as respects the sentencing power only. In all their respects, there is no difference between as Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge and an Additional Sessions Judge who has in fact been appointed as such. There is nothing in the Code to indicate any other difference. A golden rule of interpretation of statute is the plain and simple meaning rule which means that a statute should be interpreted in its plain and simple meaning. Nothing should be imported in the statute which is not there in it. Thee is nothing in sub-section (4) of section 31 Cr.P.C. or in the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 9 Cr.P.C. or in any other provision of the Code that can lead to a view that ail Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judge is to be deemed Additional Session Judge only for the purpose of passing the enhanced sentence under sob-section (4) of section 31 Cr.P.C. and is not to be deemed as Additional Sessions Judge in other respects. It may be stated here that in interpreting a statute an interpreter would least brother himself with the consequences if they inevitably follow from the words that are used. Where the meaning of the words of a statute is clear that has to be given effect to irrespective of the consequence. If, therefore, as a result of Assistant Sessions Judges being deemed to have been appointed as Additional Sessions Judges an appeal as against any judgment passed by an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge irrespective of the sentence is required to be filed in the High Court Division, and the present dispensation of the Criminal Appellate file of the Sessions Judges of the various districts would almost become nil and such cases would accumulate in the High Court Division it is not a matter for consideration of a court interpreting the law. The function of the court it to give effect to the Division of the statute following from its language. If the meaning is plain and there is no ambiguity, there is no scope for making any acrobatics of construction. In the relevant provisions of the Cr.P.C. referred to above, I do not find any ambiguity and I am led to the view that an Assistant Sessions fudge deemed to be appointed an Additional Sessions Judge can exercise all the powers and discharge all the functions of an Additional Sessions Judge, subject to the only limitation that such as Assistant Sessions Judge, cannot pass a sentence of death. It, therefore, follows that an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge is competent to heat revisional applications under sections 439A and to hear appeals under section 409 of the Cr.P.C. In the reported decision of Md. Mostafa Mandal placed before me the learned Single Judge has taken a view that an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as. Additional Sessions Judge under the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 9 of the Cr.P.C. continues to act as an Assistant Sessions Judge. only with an extended sentencing power and that the provision of section 408 of the Code which provides that a person convicted on trial held by an Assistant Sessions Judge may appeal to the Court of Sessions when the sentence of imprisonment is for a term not exceeding five years, will be attracted in all its force against any judgment passed by any Assistant Sessions Judge deemed as an Assistant Sessions Judge and appeal as against any judgment by such Assistant Sessions Judge involving conviction and sentence for a term not exceeding five years shall Ice to the court of Sessions only and not to the High Court Division. The point involved in the case before me is not whether an appeal from the conviction and sentence of an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge shall lie in case of sentence not exceeding five years to the High Court Division or the Court of Sessions. The question before me is a bit different and the question is whether the Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be an Additional Sessions Judge is competent to hear revisional applications under section 439A Cr.P.C. It is evident that the view expressed by the learned. Single Judge has bearing also on the point that has been raised before me. However, I have carefully gone through the reasonings and the view expressed by my learned brother and it appears to me that the reasonings and the view expressed by him are open to criticism. I am unable to persuade myself to take the satin view. In view of the discussions already made I am of the opinion that an Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge under the proviso to subsection (3) of section 9 is to be treated as Additional Sessions Judge, for all purpose of the Code subject to the only limitation that his sentencing, power does not extend to the imposition of the sentence of death but extend only to the imposition of sentence of transportation for life and he is competent to hear revisional application under section 439 A (3) Cr.P.C. and appeals under section 409 Cr.P.C. On merits, Mr. Formanullah Khan the learned advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Magistrate has after consideration of the evidence come to the conclusion that the second party was in possession of the proceeding shop house and there was no likelihood of breach of peace and thereafter has ordered to drop the proceeding and has passed consequential order but the learned Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be Additional Sessions Judge has, without reversing those findings of the learned Magistrate, set aside his order and has also directed the Magistrate to attach the proceeding shop-house under section 146 Cr. P.C. until determination of the dispute by a Civil court. The learned advocate submits that unless the court decides that none of the parties was in possession or is unable to satisfy itself as to which of the parties was in such possession he is not competent to attach the proceeding property and direct the parties to got to a civil court for determining the rights of the parties thereto or the person entitled to possession thereof. 

 6. Mr. S.C. Das, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, on the other hand, has submitted that the learned Magistrate has not applied his .mind to the evidence on record and his conclusion that the second party was in possession and further that there was no likelihood of breach peace is not based on evidence. Mr. S.C. Das, the learned Advocate has also contended that in the instant case since a receiver was already appointed there was apparently no likelihood of breach of peace so long as the receiver continued in possession. The learned Magistrate ought to have considered whether, there would be an apprehension of breach of peace in case the order of attachment of the property and appointment of receiver is recalled, Section 146, sub section (1) of the Cr. P. C. reads as follow;- 

 8. The question whether there is an apprehension of breach of peace is a question for decision of the learned Magistrate based on his subjective satisfaction. This satisfaction is of course a judicial satisfaction and must be based on objective materials. I have been taken through the evidence of the witnesses examined by the parties. It is  difficult to hold that there were no materials before the learned Magistrate for making the conclusion that there was no apprehension of breach of peace at the time of making the order. The proceeding was drawn as early as on .4.6.77 and the learned Magistrate made the order on 13.1.83. The passage of 5½ years of time without any in client threatening a breach of peace (there is no such allegation) was by itself a circumstance sufficient for the satisfaction of the learned Magistrate that there was no apprehension of breach of peace. The learned Magistrate has been satisfied on consideration of the oral and circumstantial evidence of the case that there was no likelihood of breach of peace. It is difficult to say that he has not applied his judicial minivan that his satisfaction is not based on materials. The proviso to section 146 (1) of the Cr.P.C. confers powers upon the Magistrate to withdraw attachment if he is satisfied that there was no longer any likelihood of breach of peace in regard to the subject of dispute and if the discretion has been exercised properly there is no case for any interference by a revisional court. Mr. S.C. Das could not place before me any authority to support his contention that before withdrawing the attachment the learned Magistrate was also reburied to consider that if the order of attachment and appointment of receiver is recalled, there would be a likelihood of breach of peace. From a reading of the proviso no such inference can be made. Mr. S.C. Das, the learned Advocate has also assailed the finding of the learned Magistrate as to possession of the second party in proceeding property. The learned Advocate submits that learned Magistrate has gone too far to look into the documents of title of the parties. The learned Advocate further submits that sub-section (41 of section 145 Cr.P.C. provides that the Magistrate shall, without reference to the merits of the claim of any of the parties to right to possess the subject of dispute, peruse the written statements of the parties, receive evidence produced by them, consider the effect of such evidence and if possible decide whether any or which of the parties was at the date of the order made under sub-section (1) of section 145 in possession. The proviso to sub-section (4) provides that if it appears to the Magistrate that any party had within two months next before the date of such order been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed he may treat the party so dispossessed as if he had been in possession on such date. Mr. S.C. Das, submits that the learned Magistrate has not considered the evidence on the point that the first party was in possession within two months next before the date of the order made under sub-section (1) of section 145 Cr.P.C. It appears that both the parties has claimed continuous possession in the proceeding house and both the parties led evidence to prove their respective cases. It appears from the judgment of the learned Magistrate that he has considered the respective documents of title of the parties and other documents only for the purpose of finding the probability of the cases of the respective parties in regard to possession. The consideration of the document of title was therefore merely incidental for determination of the question of possession and the learned Magistrate cannot be said to have no jurisdiction to consider these documentary evidence for coming to a finding about possession. The finding of possession of the learned Magistrate is on documentary and oral evidence adduced by the parties. The learned Magistrate found possession with the second party. Obviously he disbelieved the claim of possession made by the first party and accepted the second party's story of continuous possession. It is difficult to hold that the finding of the learned Magistrate is not based on evidence or is perverse. There was no reason for the learned Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be an Additional Sessions Judge to interfere with the order of the learned Magistrate and I also do not find any reason to interfere with it. 

 In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and order of learned Assistant Sessions Judge deemed to be appointed as Additional Sessions Judge in Criminal Motion No. 53 of 1983 are set aside and those of the learned Magistrate passed in Misc. Case No. 160 of 1977 are restored.
